source_refs.note: Topic 10.2, printed pages 221-223: the transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide, the Bohr effect, the chloride shift and carbon monoxide poisoning.

blocks.text: Gas transport is an essential component of respiration: oxygen is transported from the lungs to all the tissues and, at the same time, carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs.

The partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli allows it to diffuse through the alveoli into the pulmonary capillaries. Inside the blood a small amount of oxygen dissolves in the plasma, which can dissolve a maximum of only about 3 mL of O2 per litre; yet whole blood carries almost 200 mL of O2 per litre. The reason is that most of the oxygen is not dissolved in the plasma but bound to molecules of haemoglobin inside the red blood cells (RBCs).

The partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli at sea level is approximately 105 mm Hg, less than in the atmosphere, and at this pressure about 97% of the haemoglobin in the RBCs combines with oxygen to become oxyhaemoglobin, which has a bright red, tomato-juice colour. As the blood travels through the capillaries, some of the oxyhaemoglobin releases oxygen and becomes dark red deoxyhaemoglobin. When the blood leaves the tissues in the veins it has a low partial pressure of oxygen (40 mm Hg) and 75% of its haemoglobin is still saturated as oxyhaemoglobin. So 22% (97% minus 75%) of the oxyhaemoglobin has released its oxygen to the tissues, leaving 78% in the blood as a reserve. This large reserve enables the blood to fulfil the body's oxygen needs during exercise as well as at rest.

blocks.title: Why vessels are drawn red and blue
blocks.text: Oxyhaemoglobin is bright red while deoxyhaemoglobin is dark red, but deoxyhaemoglobin gives tissues a bluish tinge. Because of these colour changes, vessels carrying oxygenated blood are always shown in red and vessels carrying oxygen-depleted blood in blue. The oxygen reserve also ensures that the blood contains enough oxygen to maintain life for four to five minutes if breathing is interrupted or the heart stops pumping.

During exercise the muscles use more oxygen from the capillary blood, which lowers the partial pressure of oxygen in the venous blood to 20 mm Hg; the saturation of haemoglobin then drops from 75% to 35%. Because the arterial blood still contains 97% oxyhaemoglobin, the amount of oxygen unloaded is now 62% (97% minus 35%) instead of the 22% at rest. The CO2 produced by the tissues lowers the pH of the blood, and the lowered pH reduces haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, so it releases oxygen more readily; this effect of pH on haemoglobin's affinity is the Bohr effect. Increasing temperature has a similar effect, so during exercise, when the skeletal muscles produce more heat, haemoglobin unloads a higher percentage of its oxygen.

Blood capillaries deliver oxygen to the tissues and remove carbon dioxide from them. The partial pressure of CO2 is higher in the tissues than in the blood, so carbon dioxide enters the blood; the process reverses in the lungs, where the partial pressure of CO2 is lower in the alveoli than in the blood. The blood transports carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs in three ways.

items: As bicarbonate ions (about 72%): CO2 enters the RBCs and combines with water to form carbonic acid (H2CO3) in the presence of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase. Carbonic acid dissociates into hydrogen ions (H+) and bicarbonate ions (HCO3-). The hydrogen ion readily associates with oxyhaemoglobin, whose oxygen is released to the tissue, while the bicarbonate ions move out of the RBCs into the plasma. Their movement is facilitated by a transporter that exchanges one chloride ion (Cl-) for each bicarbonate ion, the chloride shift or Hamburger phenomenon.
As carboxyhaemoglobin (about 20%): when the partial pressure of CO2 is higher in the blood than in the tissues, CO2 combines with the globin chains of haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin.
As dissolved CO2 in plasma (about 8%): when CO2 enters the blood, a little dissolves in the water of the plasma.

blocks.text: The blood carries CO2 in these three forms to the lungs. The lower partial pressure of CO2 in the alveolar air causes the conversion of H2CO3 back into H2O and CO2, and the CO2 diffuses out of the blood into the alveoli to leave the body in the next exhalation.

blocks.title: Acid-base balance, and why O2 and CO2 do not compete
blocks.text: The formation of carbonic acid is important in maintaining the acid-base balance of the blood, because bicarbonate serves as the major buffer of the blood plasma. CO2 binds to the protein portion of haemoglobin while O2 binds to the haem irons, so the two do not compete for attachment.

blocks.alt: Two panels. Tissue end: carbon dioxide from the tissue cells crosses the capillary wall; some dissolves in plasma, some enters red blood cells and combines with haemoglobin, and some combines with water (carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which gives hydrogen ions (they combine with Hb) and bicarbonate ions; bicarbonate leaves the RBC as chloride enters. Alveolar end: the same reactions run in reverse and carbon dioxide diffuses out into the alveoli.

Tissue end: carbon dioxide from the tissue cells crosses the capillary wall; some dissolves in plasma, some enters red blood cells and combines with haemoglobin, and some combines with water (carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which gives hydrogen ions (they combine with Hb) and bicarbonate ions; bicarbonate leaves the RBC as chloride enters. Alveolar end: the same reactions run in reverse and carbon dioxide diffuses out into the alveoli; bicarbonate enters the RBC and chloride leaves.

blocks.title: Carbon monoxide poisoning
blocks.text: Incomplete combustion of fuels such as wood, gasoline, propane or natural gas produces CO gas; if gas heaters are left burning overnight in closed rooms it accumulates. Inhaled CO binds to haemoglobin with a much higher affinity than oxygen, reducing the haemoglobin available to carry oxygen and causing tissue hypoxia (oxygen deprivation). Symptoms may include headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, confusion, shortness of breath, chest pain and loss of consciousness; severe cases cause permanent brain damage and even death.
